<reason>Side A (CON) won a competitive but clear debate. A's opening scope attack—PRO's strongest material (inheritance, unconsenting children) targets germline editing while the motion concerns consenting adults—forced B to pivot to an infrastructure slippery slope, and A kept demanding a mechanism B never supplied, backing the demand with concrete counterexamples (FDA somatic approvals without germline creep, opioid scheduling rather than category-wide bans, cosmetic surgeons vs. the organ-removal ban). A answered B's pressure questions directly and principledly (self-regarding consent bars minor/parental edits), while B's best moments—the "distinction without a wall" argument and the late opioid reversal in closing (enforcement arrived only after the market was built)—kept the slope clash alive but remained predictive. B's burden-flip in the closing was under-justified. A's minor costs: a misdescribed [B2.3] concession, sloppy "C3.2/C4.3" reference labels, and a clipped opening; B suffered a clipped rebuttal 2 and never answered the licensed-permanent-elective-procedure examples. Both sides were rhetorically sharp; A made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 (A2.3) listing voluntary sterilization, living kidney donation, and elective cosmetic surgery as grave, irreversible, consented, non-therapeutic procedures demolished B's claim that medical ethics never accepts consent for such interventions; B's only reply (unlicensed experimentation on volunteers) never engaged the licensed-elective cases, leaving a live route for A that B never closed.</best_rebuttal>
